content:
I stopped doing a Bachelor's in mathematics during Covid, but I am still interested in it. I would like to try and publish a paper that I've been playing with for some time, and I am hoping that a proof assistant can help scaffold the theoretical stuff for it. I've had some experience with Rocq, and a bit less with lean4.

My more immediate goal is to formalize some stuff in optimal transport for MathLib (hopefully). My plan is to start with the play servers 'Reintroduction to Proofs', 'Real Analysis, The Game', and try and go from there. Open to any input regarding paths to achieve that immediate goal.

I think it is really cool that the community values human connection, and I hope to be able to connect with some of the people here. I don't believe I've ever been in a community that has followed the 'Contributer Covenant Code of Conduct' before, and I am excited to see how it feels in practice.

One thing that I am worried that my incompetence will be viewed as low effort.

I think as an undergrad the games are a good way to start, and perhaps Mechanics of Proof . Just keep in mind there is a bit of a journey to get to Mathlib level code ( contributors typically spend years or if full-time then many months before they are able to do so).

Incompetence is the expectation when starting, and depending on your journey here and other things you have been exposed to, it can take a variable amount of time to feel competent.

It is fairly rare for an undergrad to get involved in Lean, the community tends to have more mathematically mature members and that can be reflected in this forum, so you are already doing something fairly challenging.

People here are willing to help newcomers, but a big sticking point is AI use when beginning to learn. You will have a lot more engagement if you ask questions with "human incompetence" in your code, over something an AI produced. At the start I think it is crucial to avoid AI.

Lucas Orman said:

One thing that I am worried that my incompetence will be viewed as low effort.

You can counteract this appearance of low-effort by thinking about the question before you ask, and thinking about your response before you make it. In particular, append each with "Could I have looked this up in a manual?" before posting. If the answer is yes, don't post.

Most people here are patient with well-intentioned and well-pointed discussion, where ignorance is displayed and corrected honestly.
sender_full_name: J. J. Issai (project started by GRP)

content: Thank you for all the advice! I will keep it in mind moving forward.
